\chapter{Weather and Ground}
\label{ch:ka-weather-ground}
\hlchaptermodality{59}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the weather and the ground under it in Kannada, from the wind to the fire.}

Complete KA-C59-fire and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[gāḷi]{\kn{ಗಾಳಿ} (gāḷi) — wind, air}

\label{lesson:KA-C59-wind}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{bēḍa} mean, and what did \emph{aṣṭē} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಗಾಳಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಗಾಳಿ}} (\emph{gāḷi}) — \textquotedblleft{}wind, air\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, and it holds the moving wind and the still air on one shape. \kn{ಗಾಳಿ} \kn{ಬರುತ್ತಿದೆ} is a breeze coming up; \kn{ಗಾಳಿ} \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} in a shut room is that there is no air in it.

Now put it beside the weather-word you already have. \kn{ಹವಾಮಾನ} was built from a Persian piece meaning air and a Sanskrit piece meaning measure — a borrowed air-word for the forecast on the radio. \kn{ಗಾಳಿ} is the air on your face. The formal report and the thing itself ended up in different layers of the language, and a Kannada speaker moves between them without noticing.

\kn{ಗಾಳಿ} also carries rumour, the way English talks about something being in the air.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things the weather does to the ground.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gāḷi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{gāḷi}, then \emph{havāmāna}, and say which of the two you can feel
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಗಾಳಿ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}wind, air\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mañju]{\kn{ಮಂಜು} (mañju) — mist, fog, frost}

\label{lesson:KA-C59-mist}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{gāḷi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮಂಜು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಮಂಜು}} (\emph{mañju}) — \textquotedblleft{}mist, fog, frost\textquotedblright{}.

One word for cold water in the air, however it arrives: the fog on a \kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ} before sunrise, the mist in a valley, the frost on a leaf at dawn. Kannada did not think the difference worth a second word, which tells you something about the climate it grew up in — the state has hill country and coast and dry plain, and none of it has much use for a snow vocabulary.

The Kodagu and Chikkamagaluru hills are where this word lives hardest. Coffee country sits high enough that \kn{ಮಂಜು} is what the mornings are made of for months at a stretch.

Held up beside \kn{ಮೋಡ} the pair is tidy: the \kn{ಮೋಡ} is the water overhead, the \kn{ಮಂಜು} is the same water come down to stand among the trees.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and the second is the first one's water at ground level.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mañju}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mōḍa}, then \emph{mañju}, and say which of them you can walk into
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಮಂಜು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}mist, fog, frost\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maraḷu]{\kn{ಮರಳು} (maraḷu) — sand}

\label{lesson:KA-C59-sand}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mañju} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮರಳು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಮರಳು}} (\emph{maraḷu}) — \textquotedblleft{}sand\textquotedblright{}.

Read it slowly and you will see \kn{ಮರ} standing at the front of it. Do not trust that. The tree-word and the sand-word are separate items that happen to begin alike, and a learner who joins them has invented an etymology. Kannada has plenty of real ones; this is not one, and knowing when to stop is part of the skill.

What \kn{ಮರಳು} genuinely does share is a shape with a doing-word. \kn{ಮರಳು} also means to turn back, to return — so the same run of letters is both the sand on a river bed and the act of going home. In a chapter about taking your leave that is a happy accident and nothing more, but it is the kind of accident worth noticing, because the two are told apart by nothing except what sits around them.

The \kn{ಮರಳು} you meet most is on the bank of a \kn{ನದಿ}, where the river drops what it has been carrying.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and one warning about reading too much into a spelling.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maraḷu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mara}, then \emph{maraḷu}, and say why they are not relatives
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಮರಳು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sand\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kesaru]{\kn{ಕೆಸರು} (kesaru) — mud}

\label{lesson:KA-C59-mud}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{maraḷu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಕೆಸರು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಕೆಸರು}} (\emph{kesaru}) — \textquotedblleft{}mud\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, and unavoidable. From June onward the \kn{ಮಳೆಗಾಲ} turns every \kn{ದಾರಿ} that is not paved into \kn{ಕೆಸರು}, and a \kn{ಹಳ್ಳಿ} measures the season by how much of it there is between the house and the road.

It is also the mud a rice field wants. Paddy is planted into standing water and soft ground, so \kn{ಕೆಸರು} is not a complaint in a farmer's mouth the way it is in a city one — the \kn{ರೈತ} needs it, and a dry season without it is the bad outcome.

Then, as everywhere, it goes figurative. To throw \kn{ಕೆಸರು} at somebody is to smear their name, and Kannada arrived at that picture on its own, from a place where mud is genuinely at hand for half the year.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one the season makes.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kesaru}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{maraḷu}, then \emph{kesaru}, and say which one the rain makes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಕೆಸರು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}mud\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[beṅki]{\kn{ಬೆಂಕಿ} (beṅki) — fire}

\label{lesson:KA-C59-fire}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kesaru} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬೆಂಕಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಬೆಂಕಿ}} (\emph{beṅki}) — \textquotedblleft{}fire\textquotedblright{}.

Kannada's own, and once again it stands apart from its sisters: Tamil reaches for \emph{neruppu}, Telugu for \emph{maṇṭa}, and Kannada for \kn{ಬೆಂಕಿ}. The bone-word did this to you a chapter ago. Being close relatives has never obliged four languages to agree.

The \kn{ದೀಪ} from the asking-chapter needs this word before it is any use, and so does the \kn{ಬಿಸಿ} under \kn{ಬಿಸಿಲು}. Fire is the thing the \kn{ಗಾಳಿ} feeds and the \kn{ಕೆಸರು} puts out.

And with \kn{ಬೆಂಕಿ} the run closes the way it opened, on something you can point at. \kn{ಆಕಾಶ} was overhead and out of reach; this one is on the floor of the kitchen, close enough to warm your hands at.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \kn{ಗಾಳಿ}, \kn{ಮಂಜು}, \kn{ಮರಳು}, \kn{ಕೆಸರು}, \kn{ಬೆಂಕಿ}. Air, water, ground and the thing that undoes all three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{beṅki}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{dīpa} and \emph{beṅki}, and say which one needs the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಬೆಂಕಿ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}fire\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
